Items.Authors: Aaron Hunter, Philip Hinz, Gabriel Kruglikov
Items.Title: Control and electronics architecture for large adaptive secondary mirrors
Items.Abstract: (ASM) for the Keck 1 telescope. An ASM has advantages over an adaptive optic system at a telescope port, however, it also brings significant engineering challenges, primarily heat dissipation over the primary mirror.     This work discusses the electrical design and control system architecture for the ASM which . will have at least 2500 linear electromechanical actuators across its surface. We present designs for three different control approaches, balancing the dynamic performance of an analog driver with the lower power requirements of a pulse-width modulated driver.     Another significant challenge in ASM control is the transmission of the control signals at rates dictated by wavefront sensors (<=2KHz). We present an interface module design for parallelizing the control signals in order to meet this requirement.    Finally, we present the overview of the overall architecture and its interface to the Keck telescope.

Items.Authors: Simone Sacquegna, Gianluca Di Rico, Fernando Pedichini, Elisa Portaluri, Benedetta Di Francesco, Achille Nucita, Simone Antoniucci, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Maciej W. Bajor, Gianluca Li Causi, Roberto Piazzesi
Items.Title: Convolutional neural network for the PSF subtraction in high contrast imaging
Items.Abstract: Thanks to Adaptive Optics systems, ground-based telescopes in the 8m class have been successful in detecting exoplanets through direct imaging, starting with the infrared bands, and recently also in the visible, with the Hα observations of PDS 70 b,c and WISPIT 2 b protoplanets.  One of the hardest parts of exoplanet detection is the data post-processing, in particular distinguishing the planet signal from the speckle noise of the parent star in which it is embedded (by reconstructing and removing the PSF of the star from the image); the planet is indeed often 10^5 or more times fainter than the star.  Typical algorithms such as ADI - PCA rely on the statistical analysis of the data sequence. In this work, we are proposing the use of a trained neural network as a robust estimator of the parent star PSF, using precise simulations of telescope observations in which the PSF is generated through a complete physical optics system, generating pairs of ideal and corrupted images of the field.

Items.Authors: Riccardo Falco, Andrea Bulgarelli, Nicolò Parmiggiani, Valentina Fioretti, Eric Burns, Luca Castaldini, Elisabetta Cavazzuti, Valerio D'Elia, Laura Di Gesu, Ambra Di Piano, Tori Fae, Antonio Femia, Francesco Fenu, Wing Yeung Ma, Mattia Maniscalco, Israel Martinez-Castellanos, Ghulam Mustafa, Eliza Neights, Gabriele Panebianco, Alessandro Rizzo, Claudio Sartori, Yong Sheng, Fabrizio Tavecchio, Steven E. Boggs, Dieter H. Hartmann, Carolyn A. Kierans, John A. Tomsick, Eric A. Wulf, Andreas Zoglauer
Items.Title: COSIflow: a modular framework for orchestrating and monitoring automated scientific pipelines for the COSI mission
Items.Abstract: The Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) is a NASA mission that surveys the MeV gamma-ray sky through high-resolution spectroscopy, Compton imaging and polarisation measurements. To meet its science data processing needs and enable rapid follow-up of GRB detections, we developed COSIflow, a workflow framework extending Apache Airflow with mission-specific capabilities. Through its COSIDAG class, COSIflow standardises scientific pipeline construction and supports parallel, reproducible workflows. We present operational pipelines such as the Fast Transient Pipeline that analyse data downlinked via TDRSS after an onboard trigger, which will be based on COSIflow.

Items.Authors: Horst Steuer, Markus Feldt, Andreas Obereder, Thomas Bertram, Florian Briegel, Hugo Coppejans, Carlos Correia, Martin Kulas, Stefan Raffetseder, Silvia Scheithauer
Items.Title: Creating an ELT scale command matrix in less than a second for METIS on a consumer grade GPU using Python
Items.Abstract: METIS, the Mid-infrared ELT Imager and Spectrograph, one of the first instruments to be used at ESO’s 39m Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), will use its Single Conjugate Adaptive Optics (SCAO) system for all observing modes. An essential part of SCAO will be the command matrix which will be used to reconstruct wavefront information in the control space of the deformable mirror M4 of the ELT from measurements of the pyramid wavefront sensor on the hard real-time computer. Both, the pupil and M4, are not fixed with regard to the pyramid wavefront sensor, making an update of the command matrix every 2 seconds necessary in the worst case.  In this presentation we show that we are able to produce a command matrix on the fly in less than one second on consumer grade hardware using a single GPU by approaching the problem in an innovative way. In an end-to-end simulation we show that the approach does not compromise any accuracy and that M4 misregistration is being handled well.

Items.Authors: That Minh Bao Ton, Damien Prêle, Manuel Gonzalez, Jean Mesquida, Didier Charrier, Edouard Bechetoille
Items.Title: Cryogenic low-Flicker noise amplifier optimized for superconducting detectors in x-ray astronomy
Items.Abstract: Optimized for the Athena X-IFU, a cryogenic SiGe BiCMOS LNA addresses the critical challenge of flicker noise. By leveraging analytical models and geometric sizing, the design targets a noise floor below 1 nV/√Hz down to 1 Hz. Experimental results from a fabricated prototype confirm its suitability for superconducting detector applications.

Items.Authors: Ranjani Srinivasan, Samantha Gray, Thomas Gauron, Ryan Chaves, Manuel Fernandez, Janice Houston, Michael Johnson, Rebecca Baturin, Jonathan Weintroub, Rurik Primiani, Kazunori Akiyama, Peter Galison, Daniel Marrone, Summer Franks, John Ford, Eli A. Zervigon, Ross Mpi, Stephen Joyce, Gilles Aminot, Doug Martens, Bryan Bilyeu, Jade Wang, Vanessa Marquez, Hannah Levin, John Test, Mark Freeman
Items.Title: Data Processor Subsystem for the Black Hole Explorer
Items.Abstract: The Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) is a proposed space-based Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) mission  designed to detect and measure the photon ring surrounding a black hole, capturing light that has completed  orbits within the strong gravitational field near the event horizon. This paper describes the development of the  backend electronics for the Black Hole Explorer instrument, referred to as the Data Processing (DP) subsystem.  The functional and physical architecture of the DP subsystem is described. This includes the key design  motivations, critical trade studies, and architectural decisions made to satisfy established mission and instrument  requirements.

Items.Authors: Yoshiyuki Kubo
Items.Title: Data reduction pipeline for the PETREL CMOS sensor: row-correlated read noise removal, temperature-scaled master darks, and non-uniform flat correction
Items.Abstract: PETREL is a microsatellite designed for wide-field near-UV observations of transients. We present a specialized ground-based data reduction pipeline developed to address operational constraints, including a ±5 °C temperature drift, attitude instability, and the lack of a mechanical shutter. The pipeline incorporates row-correlated readout noise removal, temperature-scaled master dark correction synthesized from sky images, and non-uniform flat-fielding using onboard LEDs. Photometric evaluations demonstrate that this framework reduces photometric error by approximately 1.0 magnitude at a 5σ confidence level. As a result, the expected limiting magnitude is 18.6 mag(AB) in the 250-300 nm waveband with a 1000-second integration time, which satisfies the mission requirements.

Items.Authors: Isaac Dinis, Muskan Shinde, Nicolas Blind, Bruno Chazelas, Nathanael Restori, Christophe Lovis, Sylvain Cetre, Angelie Alagao, Romain Fetick, Taïssir Héritier, Vincent Chambouleyron, Benoît Neichel, Thierry Fusco, Jean-François Sauvage
Items.Title: DD4AO control law for RISTRETTO: robustness, real-time performance, and on-sky validation with PAPYRUS
Items.Abstract: DD4AO is a novel data-driven adaptive optics controller designed through frequency-domain convex optimization, balancing disturbance rejection, command constraints, and stability. We report its first on-sky validation with the PAPYRUS instrument at Observatoire de Haute-Provence on the stars Arcturus and HD137909. DD4AO maintained stable closed-loop operation during hour-long observations while continuously adapting to changing atmospheric conditions. Real-time switching with standard Integrator and OMGI controllers enabled direct performance comparisons. On Arcturus, DD4AO improved the Strehl ratio at 1310 nm by 5 percentage points, from 28.8% to 33.9%. On the fainter HD137909, gains were limited by low signal-to-noise ratio, but DD4AO consistently reduced deformable mirror stroke and suppressed vibration peaks seen with conventional controllers. These results demonstrate DD4AO’s robustness and effectiveness on-sky, marking an important step toward deployment in RISTRETTO.

Items.Authors: Xavier Coulon, Bruno Maffei, Nabila Aghanim
Items.Title: Decision-tree guided instrumental optimisation for CMB spectral distortion measurements with an FTS
Items.Abstract: The COBE/FIRAS mission showed that the CMB spectrum is extremely close to a perfect blackbody, although tiny departures known as spectral distortions are expected. The main signatures, the y-distortion and the mu-distortion, arise from energy release and provide unique information on the thermal history of the Universe that no other observable can access. I will present the latest optimisation study of FTS-based instruments dedicated to CMB spectral distortion measurements, such as the balloon-borne experiment BISOU (CNES Phase A) and the FOSSIL M-class mission submitted to the ESA M8 call. I used decision trees to explore the multidimensional space of instrumental and observational parameters and to quantify their impact on sensitivity to CMB spectral distortions and to the cosmic infrared background (CIB). These results highlight the most efficient instrument and observation optimisation strategies for designing future missions dedicated to CMB spectral distortions.

Items.Authors: Dirk Schmidt, Andrew Beard
Items.Title: Declustered: the KAOS Evo 2 DKIST MCAO real-time control system
Items.Abstract: Realtime control (RTC) for multi-conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) in the 4-meter Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) is one of the most computationally demanding tasks in astronomical AO today. Nine wavefront sensors (1k x 1k px each) and a total of ~12k cross-correlation subapertures (20 x 20 px each) must be analyzed and 3 deformable mirrors (~3.5k actuators) commanded at a rate of 2 kHz. Initially planned to use a 10-server cluster, we meanwhile accomplished to run the entire RTC in a single server with 192 AMD Zen 4 CPU cores. This is possible due to optimized programing and efficient use of these CPUs. We abandoned the cluster approach, greatly simplifying the hard- and software architecture, operational complexity and substantially saving electrical power by using only a single server.    We present the KAOS Evo 2 DKIST MCAO RTC architecture and discuss key programming techniques for efficient use of contemporary CPUs enabling fast, low-latency RTCs for very large AO systems.

Items.Authors: Alina Malow, Conor Ryan, Iryna Shevchenko
Items.Title: Deep-learning-supported depth-from-focus microscope
Items.Abstract: Compact sensor systems, such as those used in rover missions, can benefit from 3D measurement techniques if they are accurate and resource-efficient. The depth from focus (DFF) method derives depth information solely from variations in focus and requires no additional hardware beyond a camera system. Compared to classic approaches, deep depth from focus (DDFF) methods using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can reduce the number of images needed for depth estimation. This lowers both energy consumption and memory requirements. In this work, a microscope setup was upgraded with a DDFF capability, demonstrating how DDFF can be applied to the measurement of geological samples.Experimental results indicate that DDFF outperforms conventional DFF methods in depth accuracy under limited image acquisition conditions. This study highlights the potential of DDFF as a powerful tool for in-situ scientific analysis in space exploration and other compact sensing applications.

Items.Authors: Felipe Daruich, Marco Bonati, Braulio Cancino, Norman Díaz, Michiel van der Hoeven, William McBride, Jorge Parra
Items.Title: Defining reference architecture for electronics modernization at NOIRLab observatories
Items.Abstract: NOIRLab observatories operate diverse electronics and control systems developed over several decades using different technologies and engineering approaches. As these systems age, challenges related to obsolescence, maintainability, and lifecycle support increasingly drive modernization efforts.  This paper proposes a framework for developing common reference architectures to guide future electronics modernization across NOIRLab facilities. The approach emphasizes shared engineering principles, common technology standards, and reusable subsystem architectures that can be adapted to observatory-specific requirements.  Initial candidates include servo-control systems, active optics electronics, PLC-based safety and interlock systems, and detector-controller architectures. The objective is to promote a coordinated modernization strategy that improves maintainability, engineering efficiency, and long-term sustainability across NOIRLab observatories.

Items.Authors: Matthew Werneken, Danielle Frostig, John J. Piotrowski, Ana Bonaca, Phillip Cargile, Vedant Chandra, Liam Connor, Charlie Conroy, David Cruz, Peter Doherty, Daniel Fabricant, Julian Garcia, Benjamin Johnson, Hannah Levin, Mark Mueller, Hunter Snell, V. Ashley Villar
Items.Title: Defining system requirements and science drivers for Boombox, twin high-throughput spectrographs on 6.5m MMT and Magellan Telescopes
Items.Abstract: Boombox is a pair of high-throughput optical spectrographs being commissioned with the Via Survey in 2027 to provide dual-hemisphere, r=23.5 mag spectroscopy (R~1000; 355-1010 nm) of transients. With 36 fibers over 1 deg^2, high throughput, and 100 nights/yr observing time, Boombox is uniquely poised to capture the 24th-magnitude LSST sky in spectra. Boombox will drive 10% of the survey, enabling rapid follow-up to LSST and GW transients, precursor candidate studies, and statistical catalogs of faint targets across astronomy: rare transients, UV-bright SLSNe, halo stars, FRB hosts, and beyond. We present the driving system requirements for Boombox, based on the primary time-domain science and many secondary objectives. This includes science drivers and key deliverables, flowing into detailed system requirements, optical design, and hardware selections. We review instrument trade studies, inputs from the broader Via survey, and corresponding decisions made to maximize science output.

Items.Authors: Albert Ostoja-Starzewski, Thomas Hall, Elizabeth Keefe, Mason Black, Kerri Cahoy, Michael Shao, John Monnier, Leonid Pogorelyuk, Paige Forester, Carter Sweeney, Clarissa Halpryn
Items.Title: Demonstration of an adjustable 1-5 meter four-mirror piezoelectric compact delay line for space interferometry
Items.Abstract: Precise optical path difference (OPD) control is essential for formation-flying interferometer mission concepts. We consider an architecture in which one collector is merged with the combiner spacecraft, allowing meter-scale baseline variations to be compensated by an onboard adjustable delay line, relaxing formation-flying requirements, and enabling a potential two-spacecraft technology demonstration mission. We present a compact four-mirror delay line for optical space interferometry that is designed to provide an adjustable 1-5 m optical path length (OPL) range within a 2U CubeSat area. We experimentally demonstrate closed-loop control across a 20 cm optical delay range at 7 total reflections. A 35-reflection laboratory configuration corresponding to more than 5 m OPL was achieved manually, while geometric simulations indicate that the autonomous control approach can span the full 1-5 m OPL range.

Items.Authors: Wilbert Ras-Vinke, Kevin Kouwenhoven, Jochem Baselmans, Kenichi Karatsu, David Thoen, Vignesh Murugesan, Pieter de Visser
Items.Title: Demonstration of single photon counting with kinetic inductance detectors from 3.8 to 25μm
Items.Abstract: One of the major goals of modern astronomy is the atmospheric characterization of Earth-like exoplanets in the optical and infrared. Extremely sensitive detectors are required to measure the exoplanet’s faint signal down to the single-photon level with near-zero dark count rates. Especially in the mid-infrared - the target band for the Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE) mission concept - semiconducting technologies are unable to meet the requirements. Therefore, we demonstrate single-photon counting with superconducting, Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors at the wavelengths 3.8, 8.5, 18.5 and 25 μm and measure dark count rates of 3, 6, 20 and 22 mHz with resolving powers (E/δE) of 9.9, 6.0, 3.2, 3.3, respectively. These results demonstrate the MKID detector technology in the mid-infrared and the intricate measurement setups required. We discuss how the detector design and measurement setup can be further optimized to improve the detector performance in the mid-infrared.

Items.Authors: Dylan M. McKeithen
Items.Title: Deriving wavefront and pointing stability requirements for SHERA using a differentiable two-mirror dLux forward model
Items.Abstract: We present a differentiable Fresnel optical model to derive wavefront and pointing stability requirements for the proposed SHERA (Searching for Habitable Exoplanets with Relative Astrometry) SMEX mission, which will use a diffractive pupil for micro-arcsecond relative astrometry of nearby Sun-like binaries to search for rocky exoplanets. Implemented in the dLux framework, the model propagates between the primary pupil, an intermediate pupil at the secondary mirror, and the detector, capturing spatially varying wavefront error (WFE) and beamwalk across the secondary. We perform parameter inference in the eigenbasis of the Fisher information matrix for the joint parameter space to suppress degeneracies that drive astrometric bias. Simulated observing campaigns then map WFE and pointing jitter into astrometric precision, yielding nominal stability requirements consistent with SHERA’s performance goals.

Items.Authors: T. Lapucci, L. Busoni, A. Puglisi, M. Bonaglia, S. Strobele, N. Devaney
Items.Title: Design and implementation of a new PLC-based driving electronics for the NACO deformable mirror
Items.Abstract: The MORFEO Test Unit (TU) will perform several tests to verify different functionalities of the AO system prior to shipping to the ELT. Although it will not be possible to evaluate system performance using input beams that fully replicate atmospheric conditions and ELT mirrors, it will be possible to assess performance when MORFEO closes the AO loop with an external deformable mirror, as in the telescope configuration. Among the available deformable mirror options, the MORFEO consortium identified the DM previously used in the NACO adaptive optics system on the VLT as a suitable candidate. This solution requires redesigning the interface between the NACO high-voltage DM amplifiers and the modern systems currently used in the ELT and VLT telescopes. The goal of this work is to design, develop, and test new low-voltage electronics to drive the DM amplifiers. This paper details a system implemented to meet the ELT's new elctronic standards.

Items.Authors: Fernando Angeles, Luis A. Madrigal, Jorge Fuentes, Jaime Ruíz-Díaz-Soto, Leonardo Garcés, Alejandro Farah, Sebastian F. Sánchez
Items.Title: Design and optimization of a closed-loop liquid cooling system for an EMCCD camera operating under low illumination and extreme environmental conditions
Items.Abstract: This work presents the design and implementation of a critical subsystem for EBANO, a low-cost integral field spectrograph. While EBANO's main components are 3D-printed, its EMCCD camera requires extreme thermal stability for optimal performance. To address the significant heat generated by the detector's Peltier (TEC) system, the team developed a specialized liquid cooling system. The primary achievement of this system is its ability to maintain an exceptional temperature stability of 0.01 °C at the detector. The summary covers the thermal requirements, the mechanical design of the heat sink, and establishes this cooling system as essential for the success of the EBANO instrument.

Items.Authors: Can Chen
Items.Title: Design and test of a time-varying X-ray source for eXTP-SFA X-ray telescope
Items.Abstract: In order to evaluate the timing performance of the Spectroscopy Focusing Array (SFA) telescopes, an time-varying X-ray source based on a grid pole-controlled X-ray tube was designed and integrated into in the 100-m X-ray Test Facility in China. This time-varying X-ray source can generate pulsed X-rays with short duration (e.g., 100 ns) or any X-ray light curve. In this report, we will present the design of the time-varying X-ray source and the test results of not only the SFA telescopes but also some already launched X-ray telescopes (GECAM, EP), including time resolution, time accuracy calibration (in Pulse mode), and time-varying response (in Light Curve mode).

Items.Authors: Sebastian Remi, Joshua Konstantinos, Cody Hopper, Wesley Fues, Sony Cheriyan
Items.Title: Design and validation of a pulse-tube cooled astronomy camera for large format detectors with sub-micron sensor stability
Items.Abstract: Teledyne Digital Imaging develops highly sensitive CCD and CMOS sensors for astronomy and integrates them into complete off‑the‑shelf camera systems. As sensor size increases, however, cooling based on thermoelectric coolers can become overly complex and inefficient at achieving sufficiently low and uniform dark current performance.  Here we present recent technical developments integrating an e2v CCD‑C6 sensor into a new camera system using a Thales 9310 pulse tube cryocooler. We demonstrate a design that provides high cooling efficiency while avoiding temperature gradients with relatively low system complexity. A layered combination of passive and active vibration mitigation is used to eliminate cryocooler‑induced camera MTF degradation. The system achieves excellent sensor stability, with ≤0.5 µm displacement using the first passive layer alone. The cooling architecture is readily adaptable to other detector types, including hybrid CMOS infrared detectors.

Items.Authors: Christian Körnig, Nicolas M. Barrière, Maximilien J. Collon, Henric Krawczynski, Shravan V. Menon
Items.Title: Design of Kirkpatrick-Baez silicon pore optics for compact hard x-ray telescopes
Items.Abstract: Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) optics offer an alternative to Wolter-I designs for X-ray imaging by using  two orthogonal reflections, eliminating the need for sagittal curvature. This makes them well suited  to Silicon Pore Optics (SPO), where flat silicon plates are bent and stacked to form lightweight,  high-performance mirrors. In conventional Wolter-like SPO, the minimum achievable bending  radius and associated internal stress puts limits on the minimum radius and consequently the focal  length. Adopting a KB geometry removes this constraint, expanding the applicability of SPO to  smaller apertures, shorter focal lengths, and shallower incidence angles, well suited to realizing a  high angular resolution hard-X-ray optics. A flexible Geant4 -based KB-SPO ray tracing code has  been developed and used to investigate design trade-offs.

Items.Authors: Xiaoxia Qiu, Chao Liu, yonghui hou, Teng Xu
Items.Title: Design of RBF-PID adaptive control strategy for nonlinear compensation in AO system
Items.Abstract: The adaptive optics (AO) system is the core technology that enhances the imaging resolution of ground-based telescopes.The control accuracy of AO systems directly determines the high-resolution observation capability of telescopes.In view of the technical bottleneck of the existing AO systems, which mostly adopt simplified control laws and fail to fully consider the time correlation of atmospheric turbulence, resulting in insufficient suppression of nonlinear disturbances and limited improvement in imaging quality,this paper aims to propose an optimized control method for AO systems that takes into account both adaptive capabilities and control accuracy.This paper designs an adaptive PID control strategy based on Radial Basis Function (RBF) neural network (RBF-PID).The core utilizes the strong nonlinear approximation capability of the RBF neural network to adaptively identify

Items.Authors: Megan M. Dubay, Henry Corbett, Thomas Procter, Nicholas M. Law, Alex Bucheli, Jonathan Carney, James Dockery, Shannon Fitton, Lawrence Machia, William Marshall, Michael Ronco, Donovan G. Schlekat, Alan Vasquez Soto, Glenn Walters
Items.Title: Design of the Argus Array Operations Database and Hardware Management System
Items.Abstract: The Argus Array is an 8m class all-sky survey instrument that will image 8,000sq-deg at 1.0”/scale as quickly as once a second. The 1200-telescope system presents challenges in hardware inventory management, real-time state monitoring, and operational coordination like those of global telescope networks, but at a scale of monitoring thousands of individual components. We have developed a PostgreSQL relational database serving as the central repository for hardware configuration, telemetry, and performance metrics. The database models complex relationships between device types and their specialized characteristics. The operations database integrates bidirectionally with the control system, providing configuration data at startup while receiving continuous state updates during operations. Hardware management is facilitated through an internal custom Jira Service Management integration. Here we discuss the database design and its implementation during the construction phase of the survey.

Items.Authors: Pruchaya Sonnapapat, Supachai Awiphan, Sasikan Suriyot, Warakon Sribunrueang, Kenwit Phimprasong, Weerapot Wanajaroen, Apirat Prasit, Pongpop Sukanunta, Thansita Thomrungpiyathan, Naphat Muangnin, Natthapong Sanwongwan, Picha Ruenarrom
Items.Title: Design of the NARIT 0.8m Ritchey–Chrétien Telescope optical tube assembly
Items.Abstract: The National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand (NARIT) presents the development of its first domestic telescope, a 0.8-m Ritchey–Chrétien system with a 15.6-arcminute field of view and a 309-mm back focal distance. The mechanical design and optimization of the primary mirror (M1), secondary mirror (M2), folding mirror (M3), elevation ring, and truss structure are detailed. This telescope is planned for use in public outreach activities and will also serve as a foundation for Thailand’s future telescope technology development. Finally, this paper aims to provide a basis for the design of similar telescopes.

Items.Authors: Julien Storm, Gert Raskin, Bart Vandenbussche, Hugues Sana, Sibo Van Gool, Pierre Royer, Maddalena Reggiani, Dirk Vandepitte, Leonardo Peri, Louis Storm, Dominic Bowman, Camille Pirat, Jorg Versluys, Mathijs Arts
Items.Title: Design, assembly, and alignment strategy of the CubeSpec Off-axis Cassegrain Telescope
Items.Abstract: CubeSpec is a 12U CubeSat mission designed to demonstrate high-resolution spectroscopy from a compact platform. The mission is now in construction phase with launch readiness early 2027. We present the design, assembly and alignment strategy, of the compact off-axis CubeSpec Cassegrain telescope, feeding the CubeSpec high resolution echelle slit spectrograph. The telescope is installed in a 12U CubeSat and features a parabolic primary mirror (M1) and hyperbolic secondary mirror (M2), achieving a focal length of 1600 mm (F/8.33 - F/17) with a rectangular entrance aperture (94×192 mm) to maximize light collection. The off-axis configuration eliminates central obscuration and simplifies mechanical mounting.

Items.Authors: Jón E. Guðmundsson, Thomas J. Gascard, Miranda Eiben, Rustam Balafendiev, Ashesh Khatua, Xiaodong Ren, Eve Vavagiakis
Items.Title: Design, assembly, and initial test results of a cryostat for holographic testing of microwave telescopes
Items.Abstract: We present the design, assembly, and initial test results of a 4-Kelvin cryostat developed for characterization of the Taurus balloon-borne microwave telescopes. The cylindrical cryostat, approximately 1.5 m in diameter and 1.0 m in length, consists of three thermal stages: a 300-K vacuum vessel, a 40-K radiation shield, and a 4-K cold stage. The two cryogenic stages, each mechanically supported by six thermally isolating G10 flexures, are cooled by a Bluefors PT420 pulse-tube cryocooler. The cryostat provides sufficient volume to perform holographic measurements of the full three-lens refractor optical systems designed for the Taurus experiment as well as other refracting systems for the cosmic microwave background. We discuss thermal and mechanical design aspects and present early results from cryogenic testing. The system represents the first cryostat ever built in Iceland.

Items.Authors: Jacob Payne, Casey T. DeRoo
Items.Title: Designing compact x-ray optics with multilayer coatings for pulsar-informed navigation
Items.Abstract: Millisecond pulsars exhibit predictable long-term stability, comparable to atomic clocks, and can serve as natural beacons for autonomous position and timing systems. Multi-layer coatings can give flexibility to telescope geometries by providing reflective efficiency greater than 20% at grazing incidence angles greater than 3 degrees, and with Bragg reflection at 45 degrees. We present the results from phase-resolved spectral analysis of NICER measurements for a set of millisecond pulsars that are prime candidates for Pulsar-informed Navigation (PIN). This analysis identifies the energy bands to enhance the signal to noise ratio of the pulsed emission. Customized multi-layer coatings can be designed to reflect photons at this energy across a wider range of grazing incidence angles, enabling shorter focal lengths for more compact telescopes. We discuss the design implications of the phase-resolved spectra on the optics and multi-layer coatings for a PIN instrument.

Items.Authors: Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Matthijs Mars, Louis Desdoigts, Jared R. Males, Joseph D. Long, Rico Landman, Olivier Guyon, Sandrine Juillard
Items.Title: Detecting rocky exoplanets within minutes with the next generation of Extremely Large Telescopes and telemetry-based post-processing
Items.Abstract: Every high-contrast imaging system needs to use post-processing to remove residual starlight from its measurement. Many algorithms lose performance at close separations due to the small diversities. We propose to use telemetry-based post-processing (TDI) where we use the information of all wavefront sensors in the system together with the science instrument to predict the stellar speckles. These can then be subtracted from the actual measurement. This approach reaches the photon noise limits at optimal efficiency without any required prior knowledge of the exoplanet. An end-to-end model is used to predict the performance of the upcoming extremely large telescopes. We will discuss the results and show that the ELTs can characterize many nearby exoplanet within minutes and that they could potentially achieve similar performance as space-based high-contrast imaging systems.

Items.Authors: Eckhart A. Spalding, Thomas Birbacher, Felix Dannert, Adrian Glauser, Jonah Hansen, Maximilian Kirchhoff, Sascha Quanz
Items.Title: Detector considerations for the LIFE mission
Items.Abstract: The Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE) is a formation-flying mission for enabling the detection and characterization of potentially dozens of Earth-sized planets at thermal infrared wavelengths. The mission will need to sieve science signals which are many orders of magnitude fainter than competing systematics, and the science detector itself will contribute potentially highly variable noise terms. We present requirements for detector read noise, quantum efficiency, and other detector characteristics, for observations of potential LIFE targets. We compare mission needs with detectors available on the market, or in development, and include a discussion of the ramifications on the surrounding mission design. Expected high-level noise budgets and predicted planet yields based on detector type are presented, and we conclude with a discussion of the most relevant future avenues in detector development and eventual integration.

Items.Authors: Selina R. Howalt Owe, Michał Kossakowski, Rikke Stougaard Klausen, Alexander Cherlin, Alejandro Valverde Mahou, Søren Hauberg, Georgios Arvanitidis, Denis Tcherniak, Carl Budtz-Jørgensen, Irfan Kuvvetli
Items.Title: Detector simulation for neural network position reconstruction in the i-RASE system
Items.Abstract: The MeV gamma-ray domain suffers from poor sensitivity, motivating advanced detector and readout technologies. The i-RASE (Intelligent RAdiation SEnsor readout systems) project addresses this by combining a custom low-noise front end with FPGA-implemented, physics-informed neural networks for real-time event reconstruction in 3D CdZnTe (CZT) Drift-Strip Detectors (DSD). At DTU Space, work focuses on 3D CZT DSD design specifications, development of a physics-based detector model, and experimental validation. The framework integrates COMSOL signal simulations and Geant4 charge-cloud generation to optimize detector geometry and generate synthetic training data. Laboratory tests show that neural-network reconstruction achieves sub-millimetre FWHM spatial resolution at 662 keV, matching or exceeding conventional methods, and reduces dead zones by improving boundary position estimates.

Items.Authors: David R. Jenkins, Daniel Jodlbauer, Pierre Haguenauer, Dietrich Pescoller, Christian Patauner, Felipe Pedreros Bustos
Items.Title: Developing and operating AO RTC software for LGS R&D
Items.Abstract: Artic (Advanced Real-Time Instrument Controller) has been developed to operate the ESO/ESA CaNaPy LGS AO R&D experiment and the Microgate led ALASCA project. It has enabled the commissioning of the AO WFSs, real-time acquisition of AO telemetry data and it has been successful in running the AO operations of CaNaPy and ALASCA. It is under continual ongoing development to implement experimental operating modes. Artic consists of core real-time control processes along with high level scripting and GUI control interfaces which communicate through shared memory structures. We present a description of the Artic software, an overview of the results it has achieved so far and a look into the future experiments that will be enabled by the Artic software.

Items.Authors: Rianne Plantenga, Hendrik M. Veen, Antonius H. M. Coppens, Daniela Perez Capelo, Pieter J. de Visser
Items.Title: Developing Hf-NbTiN hybrid Kinetic Inductance Detectors for low light level observations
Items.Abstract: Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs) are promising candidates for astronomical studies with low photon intensity, like exoplanet spectroscopy, due to their high sensitivity, and the fact that they retain the color information of the photons they detect. Hybrid detector designs with high-Tc NbTiN capacitors and readout circuitry, combined with low-Tc inductors from Al or b-Ta have been demonstrated to effectively increase sensitivity by concentrating quasiparticles in the most sensitive part of the detector. However a resolving power R>100 required for Habitable Worlds Observatory is not yet achieved.    Devices with Hafnium as low-Tc inductors are predicted to have a higher energy resolution. Here we show the progress in developing Hf-NbTiN hybrid KIDs and first measurements on such device. We find an average internal quality factor of 4.76E5 at low microwave power and a surprisingly low bifurcation threshold. We also show the first measurements on the energy resolution of these devices.

Items.Authors: Phillip J. Wise, Stephen Bongiorno
Items.Title: Development and testing of a circular whiffle tree fixture for supporting full-shell x-ray optics during x-ray tests
Items.Abstract: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) produces full-shell replicated X-ray optics for scientific applications. Testing single, unmounted full-shell optics in an X-ray beamline is an important part of the development process. The intentionally thin optics distort significantly under their own self-gravity when mounted horizontally in a beamline. It is therefore necessary to develop methods for holding them in a minimally stressed, natural state. We have developed a new mounting solution that utilizes a circular whiffle-tree to apply azimuthally varying force on the exterior of the shell to minimize deformation. The circular whiffle is advantageous in that it allows for quick mounting of shells, may reduce gravity deformation compared to existing solutions, and is relatively low cost. This paper describes the design, manufacture, and testing of the circular wiffle and compares it to mounting methods currently used in MSFC’s 100-meter x-ray beamline.

Items.Authors: Ryuji Kondo, Hsien-Chieh Shen, Makoto Arimoto, Tatsuro Kanenaga, Hiro Otsuka, Daisuke Yonetoku, Shutaro Ueda, Tatsuya Sawano, Junko S. Hiraga, Takanori Sakamoto, Hiroshi Nakajima, Hiroshi Tomida, Akihiro Doi, Hideo Matsuhara, Robert Hartmann, Lothar Strüder
Items.Title: Development and x-ray detection demonstration of pnCCD driving and readout system for future satellite mission HiZ-GUNDAM
Items.Abstract: Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) are the most energetic explosions in the universe, releasing 10^52–10^54 erg of energy over durations ranging from several tens of milliseconds to several hundred seconds. HiZ-GUNDAM is a satellite mission designed to explore the early universe using GRBs as probes. Its wide-field X-ray monitor, EAGLE, consists of Lobster Eye Optics and pnCCD as focal-plane detectors. We have developed a pnCCD drive and readout system using custom electronic boards. We characterized the front-end ASIC and then connected a pnCCD image sensor (12.7 × 25.3 mm², 450 µm depletion, 132 µm pixels). We obtained dark frames, Fe-55 X-ray–irradiated images showing spot-like events and Mn-Kα/Kβ line structures and charged-particle events from an Sr-90 source. We also collected data at several temperatures (–20 to 0 °C). In this presentation, we report on the current status of pnCCD drive experiments performed with the constructed readout system.

Items.Authors: Hiroomi Hata, Naoki Isobe, Yasumasa Yamasaki, Takeru Matsumoto, Satoru Iguchi
Items.Title: Development of a foreground model for detecting global signals of the neutral hydrogen 21cm line from the cosmic dark ages
Items.Abstract: The TSUKUYOMI is a project planning to construct decameter antenna system on the Moon to observe radio waves below 55MHz with the goal of verifying the standard cosmology by exploring the Cosmic Dark Ages. It is important and critical to calibrate the foreground emission from the Milky Way and other radio sources and the telescope instrument noises which are much larger than this absorption amount, aiming to detect the neutral hydrogen 21cm line global signal.  Here we developed a software tool to convolve the Milky Way emission with beam pattern of a dipole antenna on the Moon. This talk will introduce our newly developed tool and discuss the time dependence and frequency response of the expected spectrum calculated with this tool. We also explore the possibility of detecting the global signal of neutral hydrogen 21cm line hidden in the foreground emission.

Items.Authors: Pratyush Rajaure, Ankit Sangroula, Shivaram Phuyal, Birat Prasad Subedi, Utsav Kandel, Srishant Dhakal, Rishi Ram Paudel, Ramesh Koirala, Damodar Pokhrel, Lelin Adhikari, Nin Waam Rai, Hari Ram Shrestha, Suresh Kumar Dhungel
Items.Title: Development of a low-cost observatory-grade telescope using local engineering in Nepal
Items.Abstract: We present the development of a 16-inch optical telescope designed and manufactured entirely by local engineering expertise in Nepal. The project aims to demonstrate that high-quality astronomical instruments can be constructed using regional materials, indigenous technical capability, and cost-effective fabrication processes. In doing so, we seek to establish a sustainable model for the development of research infrastructure in countries with emerging scientific communities.

Items.Authors: Fernando Gutierrez Cabrera, Luis Carlos Alvarez Nuñez, Alejando Farah Simon, Jose Leonardo Garces Medina, Arturo Renteria Lartundo, Erika Maria Benitez Lizaola
Items.Title: Development of a monitor for estimating induced seeing at the National Astronomical Observatory of Tonantzintla
Items.Abstract: The image quality obtained from telescopes can be affected not only by the external atmosphere but also by turbulence generated within the dome by thermal gradients and airflow. At the National Astronomical Observatory in Tonantzintla (OANTON), as in most astronomical facilities, available measurements are limited to external atmospheric seeing, so there is no quantitative information on the contribution of internal turbulence. To address this gap, we propose the design and installation of a monitoring system that uses a collimated beam propagated along an internal path parallel to the stellar optical path, allowing the measurement of fluctuations resulting from turbulence within the dome. This instrument will provide direct and continuous measurements of air behavior inside the telescope and will allow the evaluation of the impact of thermal and ventilation conditions on image quality.

Items.Authors: Carla Baldovin Saveedra, Boudewijn Hut, Paulus Kruger, Mark Ruiter
Items.Title: Development of a new fronted for the LOFAR telescope: decision making process during product development
Items.Abstract: This contribution reports on the challenges and success encountered during the development of a new frontend deployed in the High Band Antennas of the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), the most sensitive radio telescope operating since 2010 at the lowest frequencies observable from Earth (10-250 MHz).     The product delivered presents several improvements: increased linearity, beamformer accuracy, easier manufacturability, and robustness due to improved potting. While production costs were kept similar to the previous version.     We reflect on the project since its inception; including the decision-making process at management level that balanced external stakeholder expectations and internal operational needs and how those decisions impacted the execution of the project.

Items.Authors: Kanaho Okamoto, Tatsuya Sawano, Yusuke Munakata, Atsushi Takada, Shinya Sonoda, Mitsuru Abe, Kai Matsunaga, Soma Deguchi, Taiyo Sato, Sana Okumura, Haruki Onoda, Hiroki Yoneda, Takeshi Nakamori, Haruki Iiyama, Dai Yaegashi, Shun Suzuki, Yoshitaka Mizumura, Masaki Morita, Tomohiko Oka, Kenji Hamaguchi, Junko Kushida, Kyoshi Nishijima, Shunsuke Kurosawa, Kentaro Miuchi, Toru Tanimori
Items.Title: Development of an anticoincidence scintillation detector for SMILE-3 to investigate negative spectral lags in GRBs
Items.Abstract: Observations in the MeV energy band are a key step to investigate the origin of the diverse spectral lags in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The SMILE-3 experiment is designed to survey this energy range using an Electron-Tracking Compton Camera (ETCC). We have developed a lightweight, compact balloon-borne anticoincidence scintillation detector capable of both rejecting cosmic-ray events and detecting low-energy GRBs. The detector employs a plastic scintillator, silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), and readout electronics. We present the performance of the developed electronics and its GRB detection capability evaluated by sensitivity calculations.

Items.Authors: Vicente Westerhout, Maximiliano Torres, Esteban Vera
Items.Title: Development of an event-based Shack-Hartmann image monitor
Items.Abstract: Turbulence profiling is of great use in adaptive optics for astronomy, space situational awareness and free-space optical communications. For this reason, efforts in upgrading the replicability and mobility requirements of turbulence profilers is needed. In this work, a Shack-Hartmann image motion monitor using an event-based camera is implemented to leverage the high temporal resolution, low power consumption and low processing load of neuromorphic devices. This complies with the replicability and mobility requirements by using only components-of-the-shelf. Comparisons of atmospheric measurements between our system and the traditional SHIMM system are provided for the SEETRUE optical ground station in Valparaiso, Chile.

Items.Authors: Nabin Poudyal, Wayne Baumgartner, Sukanya Chakrabarti, Gianluigi De Geronimo, Wesley Hodge, Peter Jenke, Paul Ray, Jarred Roberts, Eric Wulf
Items.Title: Development of an FPGA-based readout system and functional characterization of a custom NSX1 ASIC for x-ray instrumentation
Items.Abstract: We develop an FPGA-based readout system for a front-end ASIC (NSX1) with 64 channels to read out a large-area silicon drift detector used in X-ray detection instruments such as the Wide Field Monitor module for the STROBE-X mission concept. The FPGA acts as a central controller for NSX1 configuration, implementing trigger handling and event sequencing, precise event timestamping, control of an external ADC for digitization, and data transfer to the host PC. The system enables comprehensive ASIC characterization; here, we demonstrate preliminary ASIC functionality and characterization tests using a calibrated pulser for two programmable linear gain responses of 375 mV/fC and 750 mV/fC. These preliminary results validate the low-noise performance of the NSX1 ASIC and demonstrate successful DAQ system integration.

Items.Authors: Chao-Te Li, Jen-Chieh Cheng, Chung-Cheng Chen, Pai-An Chen, Ta-Shun Wei, Chin-Ting Ho, Yu-Chieh Huang, Ue-Li Pen
Items.Title: Development of differential transmission for BURSTT
Items.Abstract: Bustling Universe Radio Survey Telescope in Taiwan (BURSTT) aims to build a phased array with a large field of view to detect and localize fast radio bursts (FRBs) in the local universe. Phase I of BURSTT includes a main array with 256 antennas and 2 outrigger stations with 64 antennas around Taiwan. For phase I, we used off-the-shelf components to quickly set up the array. An FRB was detected with BURSTT-256 in July 2025, which verifies the array design. As phase I is completed, to cope with phase II with much larger arrays, we developed modules with integrated circuits. Since antennas, optical fiber transmission, and Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC) are essentially differential, to avoid the use of baluns and take advantage of the development of telecommunication technologies, we adopted differential or balanced transmission. This article describes the design and testing of various differential modules that we developed.

Items.Authors: Deli Geng, Kieran O'Brien, David Barr, John Connolly, Thomas Davies, Sofia Dimoudi, James Gill-Fleming, Aurelie Magniez
Items.Title: Development of Dual Feedline MKIDs Readout Based on RFSoC 4x2 Board
Items.Abstract: The RFSoC FPGA with RF ADC/DAC and system level processor integrated on a single chip has been well used in MKIDs readout systems. For example, the MazinLab at UCSB developed an open source pipeline processing the MKIDs readout signal from the ADC to produce the photon pulse detection. Based on UCSB’s work, the MKIDs team at Durham University further added a phase stream interface to connect GPU for the real-time pulse analysis.     In fact, the RFSoC FPGA has multiple on-chip RF ADC/DAC resources capable to support more than one readout feedline. A dual feedline design would almost half the cost per detector on the FPGA side.     The RFSoC 4x2 board, although competitive with lower cost, has reduced number of the RF ADC/DAC external connections, which is not enough for two feedlines by the common I/Q RF based MKIDs readout. This presentation shows a way to connect two feedlines with a single RFSoC 4x2 board. Both the RF interface hardware and firmware design will be discussed.

Items.Authors: Diane Hascall, Margaux Lopez, Matthew Rumore, Felipe Bustos, Mostafa Lutfi, Holger Drass, Travis Lange, Sandrine Thomas, David Cabrera, Iain Goodenow, Eduardo Serrano, Jeff Barr, Charles Claver
Items.Title: Development of the computerized maintenance management system for the Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has transitioned from construction into operations, prompting the need for robust tracking of maintenance activities essential to maintaining peak performance. The LSST Camera, a complex system and the observatory’s sole instrument, has been a major component for developing Rubin’s new Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS). Beyond scheduling tasks, the CMMS must track assets, catalog inventory, and support observatory-specific workflows, requiring significant customization and integration with existing planning tools. LSST Camera maintenance needs—including routine calendar-based tasks and data-driven, condition-based activities informed by the Engineering Facilities Database (EFD)—provide key inputs for this development. This paper presents the current status of CMMS design, customization efforts, and camera-related activities that informed those decisions.

Items.Authors: Hironori Matsumoto, Hidetoshi Sakamoto, Kaito Murakami, Takuya Hosobata, Hisamitsu Awaki, Haruki Kuramoto, Shin-ya Morita, Sayana Takatsuka, Masahiro Takeda, Yutaka Yamagata
Items.Title: Development of the lightweight x-ray Wolter-I mirror using carbon fiber reinforced plastic and ultraprecision machining technology
Items.Abstract: Lightweight X-ray mirrors with high angular resolution and a large effective area are essential for clarifying the coevolution of galaxies and black holes. To realize such mirrors, we are developing X-ray optics using carbon fiber–reinforced plastic (CFRP), a light yet strong material that can be formed into various shapes. However,CFRP exhibits a finely textured surface pattern known as print-through, which makes the surface too rough for X-ray reflection. To mitigate print-through, we developed a method to form a thin amorphous NiP layer on the CFRP surface. The NiP layer is then finished using ultra-precision machining to achieve the surface smoothness required for X-ray reflection. We are currently developing a Wolter-I CFRP mirror shell. The mirror shell has an aperture diameter of 100 mm, a focal length of 2000 mm, and a segment length of 100 mm for both the parabolic and hyperbolic sections. We will present the current status of this mirror development.

Items.Authors: Mitsuyoshi Yamagishi, Shigeyuki Sako, Masahiro Konishi, Hiroaki Sameshima, Natsuko Kato, Yuki Mori, Sohei Kondo, Takashi Miyata, Kotaro Kohno, Kentaro Motohara, Takeo Minezaki, Fumi Egusa, Itsuki Sakon, Hidenori Takahashi, Takafumi Kamizuka, Kazuya Matsubayashi, Kana Morokuma-Matsui, Masataka Imai, Takashi Horiuchi, Yuki Hirao, Yuzuru Yoshii
Items.Title: Development of the summit information system for the TAO 6.5m telescope
Items.Abstract: Real-time monitoring of site conditions is crucial to conduct observations safely. Such monitoring is, however, challenging for the TAO 6.5m telescope, which is located at Co. Chajnantor, Chile, with altitude of 5640m above sea level. By overcoming difficulties due to harsh environment of this site, we are developing a summit information system to obtain environmental data at the observation site and deliver them to observers. Up to date, we have achieved real-time monitoring of weather and web-camera data at the summit from anywhere in the world. In this presentation, we overview the current components of the summit information system and future plans.

Items.Authors: Yusuke Yoshida, Kazuki Ampuku, Koki Sakuta, Makoto Yoshihara, Keitoku Yoshihira, Ryoma Tanaka, Tetsuo Kano, Naoki Ishida, Wataru Kato, Yoshitaka Inoue, Keisuke Tamura, Takashi Okajima, Kikuko Miyata, Noriyuki Narukage, Gota Yamaguchi, Shutaro Mohri, Satoru Egawa, Hiroto Motoyama, Takehiro Kume, Yusuke Matsuzawa, Yoichi Imamura, Takahiro Saito, Kentaro Hiraguri, Hirokazu Hashizume, Hidekazu Mimura, Ikuyuki Mitsuishi
Items.Title: Development of x-ray optics for the solar flare sounding rocket FOXSI-5
Items.Abstract: We have been developing X-ray optics for the 5th Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager (FOXSI-5), a Japan–U.S. joint solar sounding rocket experiment aimed at revealing particle acceleration and plasma heating mechanisms in solar flares. The previous mission, FOXSI-4, achieved the world's first X-ray imaging and spectroscopic observation of a solar flare using our soft and hard X-ray optics. For FOXSI-5, we have prepared the reused hard X-ray optics and a newly fabricated soft X-ray optics. As a result of evaluation of the hard X-ray optics, we obtained the imaging performance of HPD < 20 arcsec at 12 keV for off-axis angles up to 7.5 arcmin, and the effective area of ~ 40 mm^2 at 6 keV for on-axis rays. FOXSI-5 launched successfully on May 14th, 2026 and observed three active regions after C-class flares. We will report the latest status of our X-ray optics, which is a key to FOXSI-5.

Items.Authors: Dehua Yang, Xin He, Xiaofei Li, Yanlyu Yang, Hua Bai, Bo Li, Shihai Yang, Fanghua Jiang, Xuhao Wu, Shouwei Hu, Dongsheng Niu, Jinzhi Yu, Li Wang, Xiaoyu Kong, Shidong Shen, Yeping Li, Haikun Wen, Lingzhe Xu, Qishuai Lu, Yongjun Liang, Yuefei Wang, Xiang Jiang, Xianzhong Zheng, Xiaohu Yang
Items.Title: Development status of the 4m segmented Jiaotong University Spectroscopic Telescope (JUST)
Items.Abstract: We present the current engineering development status of the Jiaotong University Spectroscopic Telescope (JUST), a 4-meter class optical telescope designed for high-efficiency spectral surveys and time-domain astronomy. JUST utilizes a segmented primary mirror architecture delivering competitive spectroscopic capabilities. This paper details the transition from conceptual design to the critical design and prototyping phases of the telescope structure systems.  The primary mirror (M1) consists of 18 hexagonal segments. The alt-azimuth mount design, and the site infrastructure development at the Lenghu observing station. The paper also describes the mechanical implementation of the Active Optics System using a Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor.

Items.Authors: Akihiro Fujie, Shota Narasaki, Yuto Owaki, Misaki Miyake, Junji Takaki, Tomoya Hattori, Koji Hirose, Teppe Ikezaki, Akihiro Ando, Deprez Maxime, Claire Lamour, Yukio Katsukawa, Yusuke Kawabata, Toshihiro Tsuzuki, Naoki Kohara, Yoshinori Suematsu, Fumihiro Uraguchi, Hirohisa Hara, Kota Miyoshi, Hideki Kato, Toshifumi Shimizu
Items.Title: Development status of the primary mirror and pre-coating optical measurement results for the SOLAR-C EUVST
Items.Abstract: This report details the development status of the engineering model (EM) and flight model (FM) of the primary mirror for the SOLAR-C EUV Spectroscopic Telescope (EUVST), including measurements of surface figure error (SFE) with the mirror support mechanism. A bipod-based support with leaf springs was designed and implemented to minimize mirror deformation caused by mechanical and thermal loading. The validation with the EM primary mirror demonstrated that the predicted and measured astigmatism and coma abberations agreed well, confirming the robustness of the mirror support design. For the FM mirror, gravity-reversal measurements verified that the mirror’s SFE met the optical specifications.

Items.Authors: Stephanie S. Guzman, James Hoag, Sarah Gajadhar
Items.Title: Discovering the need for dedicated CMMS support for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope
Items.Abstract: A CMMS (Computerized Maintenance Management System) is a type of software that helps companies keep track of and organize maintenance work, track and monitor assets, control inventory, document procedures, and generate relevant reporting data.  In 2024, the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope was faced with the task of migrating from a discontinued CMMS platform. During the process of preparing for the migration, inconsistencies among how staff members within different departments use the CMMS became apparent. The Inouye had roughly 30 employees that regularly used the CMMS. This team was made up of technicians, engineers, and supervisors, each of whom had different needs of what they got out of a CMMS. The need for a dedicated employee with experience in software tool configuration and administration to support an accurate and timely migration, maintain consistency of use, work as a liaison between staff and the vendor, and implement new or underutilized features became apparent.
